newsitem.title: USA: Anaheim, Calif., to vote on Walt Disney expansion.
newsitem.headline: Anaheim, Calif., to vote on Walt Disney expansion.

text.p: Elected officials in Anaheim, Calif., were expected Tuesday to approve Walt Disney Co's $1.4 billion expansion of its Disneyland resort, a project that could boost southern California's economy.
At a meeting in Anaheim late on Tuesday, the five-member city council will consider the development agreement for the project.

The city council will also consider a financial agreement that would provide $546 million in infrastructure improvements to the area around the proposed theme park and for improvements to the city's convention facilities.
To help fund these improvements, the city would issue revenue bonds, backed in part by Walt Disney Co.
"This proposed agreement secures the city's economic future," said Anaheim Mayor Tom Daly. "Not to move forward would be jeopardizing our tourism industry, which is our economic base."
"I do expect approval this evening," Daly said.

Disney officials estimated that the project would create 14,500 new jobs in southern California, including 8,100 in Anaheim alone. City officials said the project would bolster its general fund because the expanded facility would draw more visitors, larger convention groups and increase hotel occupancy in Anaheim.

Disney said it intends to build the theme park, "Disney's California Adventure," next to the famed Disneyland park. Disney said construction was expected to begin in early 1997 with completion planned by the year 2001.

The first-phase expansion plans would include 750 new hotel rooms within a deluxe resort hotel, and the Disneyland Center, a retail, dining and entertainment center that will cater to guests and convention visitors.
As part of the agreement under consideration Tuesday, $546 million would be spent for local improvements, including a $150 million expansion of the city's convention center.
As part of the $546 million in improvements, $395 million in revenue bonds would be sold.
City officials said that state and federal grants and hotel and bed tax revenues would back the $546 million of proposed improvements.
Disney would help the city to maximize the proceeds from the bond issuance by providing some credit support for the bonds to protect the city's general fund.

The revenue bonds would be issued with city council approval but without a vote of the public, city spokesman Bret Colson said. However, Colson added that it was essential that Anaheim voters approve Measure B on the November 5 ballot.
Measure B would reaffirm a two percent increase in the local bed tax, which the city council approved in January 1995 without going to local voters, Colson said.
Colson said the two percent tax is a critical funding element for the infrastructure agreement. The city would not issue the bonds until after the Nov 5 election, Colson said.

"This project is the best, most cost-effective way to deliver the necessary enhancements to the tourism district surrounding Disneyland," Mayor Daly said. "We believe the expansion will increase tourism and help avoid stagnation."

The convention center in Anaheim is already one of the nation's largest and one of the busiest. But a recent study found that the convention center was in danger of losing market share as other cities have added more meeting space.
The study concluded that without an upgrade, the Anaheim convention center could put the city at risk of losing up to $3.9 million annually in revenues and economic activity.
In August, Walt Disney won approval from the city's planning commission to build its $1.4 billion project.
